A promising result from this analysis is the relationship between number of heliostats used and achieved flux. Because most of the data used in the analysis was aiming for ‘low’ flux, there is a sizable fraction that uses fewer than 100 heliostats, or roughly 45% of the available heliostats (the number of heliostats at the NSTTF is 214). Figure 7 gives a representation of how the achieved flux increases with a higher Commented [AH3]: update number of heliostats used in the test. 20 Additionally, ensuring heliostat pointing accuracy achieved an effect on maximum flux achieved when using the entire available field. Figure 8 shows that between 6/18/2025 and 7/18/2025 after heliostat pointing correction, the achieved flux almost doubled when the DNI was just above 900 W/m2. Figure 8. The existing data is not normally distributed and is not able to be transformed to a normal distribution, therefore a Kruskal-Wallis test was used to determine statistical significance in achieved flux by month. It was found that while the flux in many months was significantly different from others, February was found to have significantly higher flux than all other months except January. 21 7. SOLAR TOWER HIGHLIGHTS Core Objective The Solar Power Tower is currently supporting all aspects of Concentrating Solar Thermal on-sun research, including optics (heliostats and metrology), high- temperature receivers, balance of plant systems, heat transfer fluids/media, thermal materials, and heat flux measurements. Capability ➢ Testing receivers, materials, and systems under high solar flux conditions Heliostat Field ➢ 37 m2 ➢ 214 heliostats ➢ Completely re-mirrored in 2010 ➢ Low-iron, >95% solar-weighted reflectivity Tower ➢ 200 ft. tall tower ➢ Three test bays ➢ Beam Characterization Target ➢ 100-ton capacity elevating module Heliostat Test Bed ➢ Full-scale heliostats ➢ Novel heliostat designs ➢ High performance reflective film evaluation 22 Tower Project Highlight: Ultra-High Operating Temperature SiC Solar Thermal Air Receiver (HOTSSTAR) PI: GE Aerospace – REZA Sarrafi-Nour Summary: In the late fall of 2025, Project Lead Ken Armijo submitted his HOTSSTAR GE Air Receiver article to Sandia National communication editors for consideration in the California Communicator and Lab News. A newly established test facility at Sandia National Laboratories successfully tested a modular silicon carbide (SiC) ceramic air receiver designed by GE Aerospace Research, achieving near world-record temperatures of approximately 1,400°C. The breakthrough opens avenues for low- cost, high-temperature thermal energy systems applicable
